candidates.title: Jiangnan Shipyard wins BV approval for electric-propelled ammonia carrier
candidates.excerpt: Jiangnan Shipyard has received Approval in Principle (AiP) from Bureau Veritas for a new electric-propelled Very Large Ammonia Carrier (VLAC). The vessel concept combines ammonia-fueled power generation with batteries, fuel cells and wind-assisted propulsion. Jiangnan Shipyard, a subsidiary of China State Shipbuilding Corporation (CSSC), developed the design in-house. VLAC combines three power sources The vessel features a medium-voltage DC hybrid electric propulsion system. It integrates three power sources: ammonia-fueled generators, an ammonia fuel cell system and containerized battery energy storage. The design also features a forward accommodation arrangement. According to Bureau Veritas, the hybrid architecture is intended to improve operational efficiency. It also provides flexibility to integrate new energy technologies in the future. Four sails provide additional propulsion The VLAC design includes four foldable soft sails for wind-assisted propulsion. These will provide supplementary propulsion and help reduce the vessel’s overall energy consumption. Jiangnan’s concept therefore combines ammonia, electric propulsion, energy storage and wind power within a single vessel design. The shipyard has also designed the vessel with future upgrades in mind. Potential additions include more advanced batteries, onboard photovoltaic power generation and next-generation fuel cells.

candidates.excerpt: Skills: Understanding the train driver shortage A shortage of skilled personnel is one of the enduring challenges facing Europe’s railways, and the lack of drivers is especially acute. With EU policy leading to a more fluid competitive passenger rail landscape and rapid mobilisation needs for new entrants, the pressure to find more drivers is becoming intense. Toma Bačić sets out the problem and how it is being tackled. The Brussels-based trade association CER has warned that around 30% to 40% of Europe’s railway workforce could retire by 2035. It says that locomotive drivers are one of the most difficult professions to replace, and their shortages are becoming a limiting factor for expanding passenger and freight services across the continent. Nowhere is that more apparent than in the DACH region, where figures from the relevant railway regulatory and licensing bodies indicate that around 570 railway undertakings have the right to operate trains (passenger or freight) across some or all of the German, Austrian and Swiss networks. In Germany, the EU Agency for Railways says 34 200 train drivers were employed by railway undertakings in 2022. This compares with 63 317 valid EU train driver licences, illustrating why licence numbers alone should not be used as a proxy for the workforce figure. candidates.title: 150th anniversary of SF–LA rail connection celebrated
candidates.excerpt: LANG, Calif. — On Sept. 5, 2026, exactly 150 years ago to the day, the first rail line joining San Francisco and Los Angeles was completed. More than 300 people gathered for a commemorative event and cheered as a ceremonial golden spike was driven. Located 43 rail miles northeast of Los Angeles and 440 rail miles from San Francisco, Lang was designated as the official meeting point of the Southern Pacific Railroad work forces connecting two of California’s largest cities in 1876. The line was completed after more than two years of feverish rail laying that included crossing the famed Tehachapi Pass and Soledad Canyon. On Sept. 5, 1876, Charles Crocker, Southern Pacific’s president, traveled via a special train from Oakland down to Lang, where he personally drove a golden spike signifying the line’s completion. Now 150 years later, as part of this year’s celebration hosted by the Santa Clarita Valley Historical Society, local dignitaries were invited to speak, with artifacts from the 100th anniversary celebration in 1976 brought to Lang, including a scratch-built model of the station that once stood in town.
